Kuril Islands: Moscow and Beijing close ranks against Tokyo
As Washington courts Moscow and Beijing, Tokyo is left to manage a worsening Kuril dispute largely on its own.
While global attention remains fixed on Russia’s war in Ukraine, Moscow’s relationship with Japan has been deteriorating in ways that carry heavy implications for security in Northeast Asia.

Russia and Japan never signed a formal peace treaty after the Second World War, chiefly because of the unresolved dispute over the southern Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories. In March 2022, Moscow suspended treaty negotiations, citing Tokyo’s sanctions and other measures taken in response to the invasion of Ukraine.

In February 2026, the Kremlin went further, declaring that relations had been “reduced to zero” because of Japan’s “unfriendly stance.” Tokyo, for its part, has imposed sanctions on Russia more than 20 times since 2022, most recently on 2 October, when it banned the provision of services to 35 vessels in the “shadow fleet” that transports Russian oil.

Russia has answered with symbolism and action. Vladimir Putin’s visit to the southern Kurils for the first time in August signalled that, from Moscow’s perspective, the territorial question is settled, and on October 27 the Russian Foreign Ministry called on Japan to rethink its unfriendly policies if it wished to restore dialogue.
From China’s perspective, Russian control of the islands is preferable to Japanese control, since islands returned to Japan could one day host US military personnel or equipment.

What makes this hardening more consequential is that it is now coordinated with China. In July, Chinese and Russian naval vessels conducted joint navigation in the waters surrounding Japan and held live-fire exercises inside Japan’s exclusive economic zone.

China’s diplomatic position on the islands is also shifting. On 13 October, a Chinese delegation visited Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu, to explore joint projects, including in fisheries. Beijing’s foreign ministry framed the trip as business activity conducted by private companies, distancing the government from it, but it also stated that “the outcomes of the victory of the World Anti-Fascist War must always be respected and upheld” when asked about the visit. That phrasing echoes the language Moscow uses to justify its control of the islands, and it marks a notable departure from the 1960s, when Mao Zedong expressed support for their return to Japan.

Beijing’s actions suggest a deliberate recalibration, likely driven by what it views as Japanese militarisation and by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks on Taiwan. From China’s perspective, Russian control of the islands is preferable to Japanese control, since islands returned to Japan could one day host US military personnel or equipment.

Japan has already been pushing to strengthen its military capabilities amid a volatile geopolitical environment. Under Takaichi, the defence budget has exceeded $58 billion for the first time in the nation’s history, and in October she told parliament that Japan would “deepen concrete and realistic considerations” regarding the defence of sea lanes, including the introduction of nuclear-powered submarines. Such a step, however, remains a difficult prospect given its technological demands and the Self-Defence Forces’ serious personnel shortages.

Tokyo’s room for manoeuvre is also limited by energy. Japan holds stakes in the Sakhalin-2 oil and gas project in the Russian Far East, and roughly 10% of the liquefied natural gas it imported in 2025 came from Russia. Moscow is clearly aware of this leverage, with Putin saying last month that Russia was “interested in cooperation with Japan” and would support Japanese companies that continue to work with it.

Washington’s posture complicates matters further. As US–China relations improve and President Donald Trump pursues better ties with Putin, a more conciliatory US approach towards Beijing, Moscow and Pyongyang could leave room for further provocations aimed at Japan, whose relations with all three neighbours are deteriorating.
The combination of a frozen Russia–Japan relationship, growing Sino–Russian coordination around Japan, and an ally in Washington with other priorities leaves Tokyo in a difficult position.

Diversifying its energy supply, including through closer cooperation with Europe, would reduce Moscow’s leverage but do little to resolve the islands dispute. More broadly, the situation risks fuelling a regional arms spiral. Although public opinion and its pacifist constitution still constrain Japan, Takaichi’s electoral mandate, a worsening threat environment and growing doubts about its partner’s reliability are likely to push Tokyo further towards military options.

Beijing and Moscow, in turn, would gain greater incentive to deepen their military cooperation against what they portray as Japanese militarisation. The effects could also extend to Seoul, which, facing a persistent North Korean threat and similar uncertainty about the US alliance, may follow Japan in a more militarised direction, intensifying the vicious cycle in an already volatile region.

Greater defence cooperation between Seoul and Tokyo could strengthen both countries’ relatively precarious security situations in the region, however here too historical disagreements create obstacles and limitations for how far cooperation can go. As such, the trend towards greater militarisation seems likely to accelerate in the short term, despite the potential grave consequences.
